title: Routing requests by hand
idea: Routing means choosing the code that answers a request from its method and path. When no route matches, you reply `404`.

analogy.text: A mail room sorting letters. Each one goes to the pigeonhole for its address; a letter with no matching pigeonhole goes to the return bin.
analogy.breaks: Mail has one address; a request is matched on method and path.

points: `req.url` is the path plus the query string, like `?limit=5`. `new URL` splits them.
Match `req.method` and the path together: `GET /notes` and `POST /notes` differ.
A known path with the wrong method gets `405`; an unknown path gets `404`.
The body arrives later, in chunks. The next lesson reads it.

hero.title: How a request finds its handler

steps.caption: A request arrives. Node has already parsed its method and `url`.
`new URL(req.url, base)` separates the pathname from the query string.
Compare the method and pathname with each route, in order.
`GET /notes` fits the list route, so that handler runs.
`GET /notes/2` fits the one-note route. You extract the id yourself.
`POST /notes` has a known path but the wrong method: reply `405` with an `Allow` header listing valid methods.
`GET /nope` matches nothing: reply `404`. Every request must end in some reply.

code.title: Splitting a URL
code.caption: Edit the URL and run again. Predict each line before you press Run.

code.title: A router for /notes
code.caption: A router called five times by its own script. Step through it, then press Run.

walk.text: A small in-memory store and a `send` helper that writes a JSON reply.
Parse the URL, then split the pathname: `/notes/2` gives `notes` and `2`.
Wrong resource or extra segments: no route matches, so reply 404.
Right path, wrong method: reply 405 and list the allowed methods in `Allow`.
No id means the whole list. A missing `limit` is `null`; `??` falls back to the note count.
With an id, look the note up: `404` if it is missing, `200` otherwise.
The script sends five requests to its own server, prints each answer, then closes.

pitfalls: Never compare `req.url` to a path directly: `/notes?limit=1` is not `/notes`.
Query values are strings or `null`; convert and validate them before use.
End the route list with a fallback reply; unmatched requests otherwise hang.

quiz.why: Query values are strings, so `'2' + 1` joins into '21'. `Number` converts it. A missing key gives `null`.

takeaway: A router is `if` statements over the method and the parsed path.

starters: Why does `req.url` include the query string?
When should I return 405 instead of 404?
